questions.explanation: Relation: synonym (the two words mean the same). Begin → Start, so Finish → End. A race has a finish, but only 'end' means the same as finish.
Relation: cause-effect (the first causes the second). Cut → Bleeding, so Burn → Blister. Fire and heat cause a burn (the wrong direction); a burn causes a blister.
Relation: category-member (the second is a member of the first category). Tree → Oak, so Flower → Rose. A petal is part of a flower, not a kind of flower.
Relation: part-whole (the first is a part of the second). Leaf → Tree, so Feather → Bird. A nest is where a bird lives and 'fly' is what it does; the feather is part of the bird.
Relation: tool-user (the first is a tool used by the second). Plough → Farmer, so Whistle → Referee. A whistle makes a sound and is used in a match, but the person who uses it is the referee.

Relation: function (the first is used for the second). Umbrella → Rain, so Helmet → Injury. An umbrella protects against rain; a helmet protects against injury. A soldier or cyclist wears it, and plastic and a strap are what it is made of.
Relation: degree (the second is a stronger form of the first). Whisper → Shout, so Drizzle → Downpour. Mist is even lighter than a drizzle; a downpour is the heavy form, as a shout is of a whisper.
Relation: antonym (the two words are opposites). Shallow → Deep, so Rare → Common. 'Unusual' is a synonym of rare; the opposite is common.

Relation: sequence (the second comes right after the first). Egg → Chick, so Seed → Sprout. A chick is the next stage after an egg, and a sprout the next stage after a seed. A flower comes later, and fruit contains the seed.
Relation: cause-effect (the first causes the second). Bacteria → Decay, so Wind → Erosion. A breeze and a storm are kinds of wind, not results of it; wind wears rock away (erosion).

Relation: part-whole (the first is a part of the second). Verse → Song, so Ingredient → Recipe. A verse is one part of a song; an ingredient is one part of a recipe. The chef and kitchen are who and where.
Relation: synonym (the two words mean the same). Hostile → Unfriendly, so Hesitant → Reluctant. 'Eager' and 'confident' are near-opposites of hesitant; reluctant means the same.

Relation: degree (the second is a stronger form of the first). Content → Ecstatic, so Uneasy → Terrified. 'Nervous' is about as strong as uneasy; terrified is the extreme form, as ecstatic is of content.

Relation: effect-cause (the first is left behind by (is the result of) the second). Ash → Fire, so Scar → Wound. Ash is what a fire leaves behind; a scar is what a wound leaves behind. Skin and face are where the scar is.

Relation: function (the first is used for the second). Anchor → Ship, so Leash → Dog. An anchor holds a ship in place; a leash holds a dog in place. The owner holds the leash (the user, not the thing held), a walk and a park are where it is used, and rope is what a leash is like.
